html:
SMTO-BOOT-0005 — SMTO needs OpenSSL to set up a secure (HTTPS) connection

GUID: 88ec7ba9-cb1f-4d18-a4c9-2435fbcefdab
Slug: boot-openssl-missing
Domain: BOOT · Subsystem: boot

What happened

  • SMTO was started with HTTPS turned on and needed to create a security certificate, but the OpenSSL tool it uses for that isn't installed. SMTO stopped instead of starting without HTTPS.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Run ./install.sh again from the project folder. The installer's list of system tools includes OpenSSL, so rerunning it adds the missing tool.
  2. Or install OpenSSL with your system's package manager (it is usually called openssl), then open a new terminal window. SMTO looks for the openssl command when it starts, and a new terminal picks up newly installed tools.
  3. Start SMTO again with the same HTTPS option, for example ./startup.sh --https. With OpenSSL available, SMTO can create the certificate it needs and start securely.

What success looks like

  • SMTO starts and you can open it with an address that begins with https://.

If it still fails

  • Copy the full terminal message, including the Error reference line, and send it to the person who manages SMTO; ask whether this copy of SMTO needs updating, because newer versions create the certificate without OpenSSL. Don't turn HTTPS off to get past this; people and Gateways may rely on the secure connection.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • An HTTPS launch needed to create a self-signed certificate because no certificate/key pair existed, but command -v openssl found no openssl executable on the launcher's PATH (only older startup.sh versions run this check; the current Server creates the pair itself).

What this means

  • HTTPS setup calls command -v openssl and finds no usable executable on its PATH. Bootstrap diagnostics report the existing installer/launcher check only. They do not download packages, probe hardware, stop processes or change state while rendering; earlier setup steps may already have modified the environment.

Why this can happen

  • HTTPS setup calls command -v openssl and finds no usable executable on its PATH.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect PATH and the supported host dependency installation, independently of certificate contents.

How to fix it

  • Install the openssl package (install.sh includes it in its system package set) so it resolves on the PATH of the account running the launcher, or provide an existing pair through AOR_SSL_CERTFILE and AOR_SSL_KEYFILE, then rerun startup with --https. Current startup.sh no longer calls openssl (smto_runtime/server_tls.py generates the certificate), so this error indicates an older launcher; updating SMTO also removes the dependency. Do not disable AOR_SSL_ENABLED to bypass the check.
  • Install the supported OpenSSL dependency and rerun HTTPS setup. Keep the intended secure transport enabled.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The setup entry point resolves OpenSSL and performs its intended secure certificate setup.

What not to do

  • Do not remove retained state or weaken trust checks to make an unavailable dependency appear healthy.

Technical notes

  • Bootstrap diagnostics report the existing installer/launcher check only. They do not download packages, probe hardware, stop processes or change state while rendering; earlier setup steps may already have modified the environment.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
